0. WHAT DØG-5 IS

DØG-5 turns the M-VAVE FM-1 pocket synth into an aggressive, live, virtual-analog voice for the band DØGS (bubblegum egg punk / garage psych). It is an 8-voice analog-style polysynth with a four-stage "Psych Chain" effect engine and a hard-chopping performance architecture built for the stage.

The one idea: the on-screen character is a dog, and his bark is the live oscilloscope — the real waveform of whatever you're playing fires out of his open mouth. The sound you shape is the sound of his bark.

Two rules govern everything:

  • TONE IS KING. Features are negotiable; tone is not. A patch that isn't right by ear doesn't ship.
  • This is a LIVE instrument. Everything is built to be played in the dark, mid-performance, without menu-diving.

PART 1 — THE PANEL

1.1 Buttons / the 12-pad command grid

DØG-5 uses page-family buttons: tapping a family button cycles through its pages, and each page maps the four knobs to four parameters. Every button also has a "dog name" (the live performance register); the printed panel label is what's physically on the unit.

Top row — synthesis & modifiers

Button Dog name What it does
FX — Psych Chain family. Tap cycles DRIVE · BBD DELAY · SPRING · TAPE. Hold = the four effect macros on the knobs (GROWL · ALLEY · DRAIN · CHEW), on any page.
SEL (dial + press) FETCH Turned on HOME (no button held): the LFO RATE of the patch, 2 steps a click, saved with the patch; it shows as a dial labelled LFO at the top left of the scene (see 1.8). Turned anywhere else: nothing. Held on a Psych page: the knobs become that effect's secondary controls. With SAVE armed, pressed: randomise (new sound).
ENV HOWL Envelopes family. Tap cycles FILTER ENV · AMP ENV.
LFO PANT Modulation family. Tap cycles LFO · LFO DEST · LFO +.
EDIT DIG Voice family. Tap cycles OSC 1 · OSC 2 · MIXER · OSC MOD · FILTER · FILTER + (on release). Hold EDIT + a black key jumps straight to a page (see 1.5).
GLO FLEAS System family. Tap cycles GLOBAL · VOICE · VOICE + · OUTPUT. The GLOBAL page carries the CPU reading (see 1.6) and the FLEAS dial (see 1.8).

Bottom row — performance & transport

Button Dog name What it does
HOME — Tap (acts on release): back to the live PERFORM page, the dog's scene. Hold: the control map of the page you are on (every knob and button, with its dog name and panel label); let go and you stay on the page. While a family button is held, tap HOME to lock that layer open; that button releases it.
SAVE BURY Tap to arm, tap again to save. Armed, the header shows the slot it will save into and what is there now (SAVE HERE?); turn PRESETS to pick another slot. Factory slots 1–32 are locked, so on one of those SAVE offers the first free slot from 33. Armed does nothing for 3 seconds: it lets go. See 1.9.
ARP ZOOMIES Arpeggiator page / on-off. On the ARP page, the ARP button also toggles HOLD (the same latch as REC).
REC WAG HOLD, on any page: press to latch the notes you are holding (they keep sounding after you let go), press again to release them. The REC light shows it. A drone latch: with the arpeggiator OFF, held notes simply ring. It is the same latch as the ARP button on its page and works alongside a sustain pedal. Changing patch does not release it; STOP does, and so does a MIDI panic ("all notes off" / "all sound off", CC 123 / 120, from a keyboard or DAW).
PLAY/STOP HEEL Global kill switch (see 1.3). It also releases HOLD.
SEQ FLOP Tape Stop (see 1.3).

Left panel

Control Dog name What it does
PRESETS BARKS Load a preset slot, instant, no confirm. With SAVE armed: picks the slot to save into (33–99 only).
ALGORITHM SLOBBER Vintage Slop ride (see 1.3).
MASTER — Master volume.
OCT− / OCT+ — Octave −2..+2 (both pressed = 0).

The hold-HOME control map lists the three tricks (HEEL STOP, FLOP TAPE STOP, SLOBBER SLOP RIDE) and WAG HOLD. To fit the screen it leaves out the HOME row itself and the FX-held macros (both are in this table).

Four knobs, contextual to the page showing. Each parameter page shows its four knobs and their values, and draws what they affect. On HOME a turned knob pops up as a dial over the scene for a moment (see 1.8). The bottom bar always shows only the preset number + name. Hold HOME for a live control map of the current page.

EDIT FILTER + KEY TRK VEL>FLT VEL>AMP —
ENV FILTER ENV ATTACK DECAY SUSTAIN RELEASE
ENV AMP ENV ATTACK DECAY SUSTAIN RELEASE
LFO LFO SHAPE RATE DELAY PHASE
LFO LFO DEST PITCH PWM FILTER AMP
LFO LFO + PITCH> PWM> — —

GLOBAL's knobs are settings for the whole unit, not the patch: TEMPO, FLEAS (the screen, see 1.8), the MIDI channel (OMNI or 1–16) and TUNE. The CPU reading sits at the top of the GLOBAL page (see 1.6).

MIXER's DRIVE is the per-voice drive in front of the filter (the gentle warmth), not GROWL. MORPH only acts when the filter TYPE is SEM (it sweeps that filter from low-pass through notch to high-pass); on the other types it does nothing.

Hold SELECT on a Psych Chain page for its secondary controls: DRIVE → BIAS · TONE · BBD DELAY → SYNC (the note value) · FINE · PINGPONG · SPRING → SIZE · DAMP · PRE-DLY · TAPE → WOW/FLT · HISS · DROPS.

The tempo (the arpeggiator and a synced delay) is GLOBAL knob 1, or an incoming MIDI clock. There is no tap tempo.

1.3 The live "trick" controls

Three controls built for live chaos, independent of the patch you're on:

  • PLAY/STOP — Global kill switch (HEEL). A live panic button. One press and everything stops in a few milliseconds: voices, and every effect buffer (delay, reverb, tape) flushed clean, so nothing rings on. Instant dead air — for a band stop, or when the delay runs away. Press again to resume. It also lets go of HOLD.
  • SEQ (held) — Tape Stop. Hold it and the whole sound drags down to a halt like a tape machine or turntable losing power: pitch, brightness and all — voices, delay repeats, reverb tail and tape hiss dive together. Release and it snaps straight back. The dog's beam dives with it.
  • ALGORITHM — Vintage Slop ride (SLOBBER). A live knob that rides the per-voice tuning instability up on top of whatever the patch already has. Clean and stable at zero; wound up full, it's worn, drifting, seasick. Never saved — resets to zero at power-up, like a master knob. At full ride, a held single note sits about 20 cents flat (a chord about 3 cents flat); that detune is the character, not a fault.

1.4 The signal path & architecture

VOICES → DRIVE (GROWL) → BBD DELAY (ALLEY) → SPRING (DRAIN) → TAPE (CHEW) → TAPE STOP → MASTER GATE
  • 8 voices. Modes: POLY, DUAL, UNISON, MONO. Variable polyphony (POLY knob, 1–8, default 5).
  • Per voice: two oscillators (saw / pulse / both), hard sync, cross-mod, noise, a filter with drive (LP 24, LP 12, HP, BP, notch or SEM: see TYPE in 1.7), two ADSR envelopes, and "Vintage Slop" (per-voice tuning/drift instability). There is no triangle oscillator; a narrow pulse through a key-tracking low-pass is the nearest.
  • One LFO per patch: everything it is routed to moves at the same rate. It cannot be tempo-synced.
  • The Psych Chain sits after the voices, reached by FX. It is the DØG-5 dirt: Drive, a free-time bucket-brigade delay, a spring reverb, and tape degrade. The tape stage is last, so it wobbles the finished wet mix: a delay repeat is pitched by the tape's state when it arrives, and everything wobbles together (a real tape echo warps each repeat separately; this cannot).
  • The bank: 99 slots. THE POUND (1–32) are the factory patches, locked: you can play and change them, but a save never lands on them (see 1.9). THE PACK (33–99) are yours to save into; an unused one starts as the INIT sound (slot 32's engine defaults at VOLUME 100).

1.5 The keybed shortcuts (hold EDIT + a black key)

The FM-1 prints a second set of labels on the keybed's upper (black) row, left to right: OP1 OP2 OP3 · OP4 OP5 · OP6 PIT GLO · MONO POLY, with one unlabelled key to the right of POLY. Hold EDIT and press one of them to jump straight to a page, wherever you are:

Key Goes to
OP1 OSC 1
OP2 OSC 2
OP3 MIXER
OP4 FILTER (press again: FILTER +)
OP5 VOICE
OP6 VOICE +
PIT OSC MOD
GLO GLOBAL (press again: OUTPUT)
MONO / POLY sets the patch's voice MODE to MONO or POLY (the header shows MODE MONO)

While EDIT is held these keys never play a note and send no MIDI. The key right of POLY always stays a note. A jump also becomes the page EDIT (or GLO) returns to next time. A plain tap on EDIT still cycles its pages, on release; if you used a shortcut during the hold, the release does not cycle. (In the browser player: hold - for EDIT and press a black-key letter; a mouse alone can't hold two things.)

1.6 The CPU meter (it is already there)

Press GLO once (it opens the GLOBAL page, the first in the GLO family). The top of the page reads CPU <n>us: how long the engine took to render the last chunk of audio, in microseconds. The source states the budget is 5800 µs for each chunk. The nearer the number is to 5800, the less room is left for the patch, the held notes and the Psych Chain together. It measures only the audio render; the screen, knobs and buttons run separately.

What was measured on Vincent's unit (12 Nov, readings drift by about ±100 µs; all four Psych Chain effects pushed hard — GROWL 82, ALLEY 443 ms, DRAIN 83, CHEW 85): with no note held the meter reads about 2700–3200 µs; with four notes held, 4500–4900 µs on most patches and about 5600 µs on 30 THE DØG. Playing 30 at that level the screen, knobs and sound all responded normally. Since the screen art (v0.4, 20–21 Nov): ordinary playing reads no higher than about 3000 µs, and FLEAS at MANGE does not raise it: the scene does not slow the sound. Not tested: more than four notes, any reading above 5800, and what happens past the budget. So this manual does not promise what happens there. The Psych Chain's crackle and dropout are part of the sound.

1.7 The steering knobs, in plain words

There is no room on the screen for explanations, so they live here. These are the knobs that change a sound the most:

  • CUTOFF — how bright the sound is. Down = darker and rounder, up = brighter and more open.
  • RESO — how much the filter rings at the cutoff. Up = a sharper, whistling edge; near the top it sings on its own.
  • ENV AMT — how hard the filter envelope sweeps the cutoff on each note. The middle (64) = no sweep; above it the sound opens with each note (a "wow" or a bite), below it the sweep goes the other way.
  • RELEASE — how long a note rings after you let go of the key.
  • LFO RATE (the SELECT dial on HOME) — the speed of the patch's one wobble, whatever it is routed to.
  • TYPE — the filter's shape: LP 12, LP 24 (darker, steeper), HP 12 (takes the low end away), BP 12 (a narrow, nasal band), NOTCH (a hole in the middle), SEM (a sweepable filter: see MORPH).
  • MORPH — only on TYPE SEM: sweeps the filter from low-pass (0) through notch (64) to high-pass (127).
  • GROWL · ALLEY · DRAIN · CHEW — the four Psych Chain effects: drive, echo, spring reverb, tape. Hold FX and all four are on the knobs, on any page.

1.8 The screen

Power-on: the boot animation. About 6 seconds: the head, the colours cycling, DØG-5, then it melts and burns through to your patch's scene. Press any key or button and it skips straight to playing.

HOME is the dog's scene. Each patch lives in one of four chapters, and HOME shows that chapter's painting with the dog in it:

Slots Chapter Accent colour
1–8 I JALOPY Sun Yellow
9–16 II BEE-TCH Wave Turquoise
17–24 III MOONSHINE Foam White
25–32 IV ACID CAN Acid Chartreuse

THE PACK (33–99) runs through the same four in blocks of eight, and a patch you save keeps the scene it was saved from: save a Moonshine sound into 50 and slot 50 is Moonshine.

  • The dog rests and sways while nothing plays. Play a note and he barks. In MOONSHINE, hold the note: he barks, draws breath, then howls.
  • The beam is the live waveform of what you are playing, fired from his mouth to the top-right corner, in Acid Chartreuse in every chapter. It is the true signal: nothing on the screen (FLEAS included) ever touches it. Hold SEQ for Tape Stop and the beam dives with the sound.
  • The top bar is the fence. It shows the voice mode and filter type, then ARP, FX (an effect is up) and HOLD when they are on, plus the chapter's name, and it carries short messages (SAVED, STOPPED (PLAY), MODE MONO, the SLOP ride). Where the bark lands, the fence breaks, each chapter its own way: Jalopy scorches it, Bee-tch soaks it, Moonshine fogs it, Acid Can wrecks it. When the sound stops it heals within about a second.
  • The bottom bar is the patch number and name. Nothing ever breaks it.
  • The dial. Turn a knob on HOME (CUTOFF, RESO, ENV AMT, RELEASE, or SELECT for the LFO rate) and it pops up at the top left as the panel's own round knob: its name, how far it is turned, its value. It goes 1.2 seconds after your last turn. (In BEE-TCH it covers the dog's tail while it shows.)

FLEAS — how mangy the screen gets. GLOBAL knob 2, 0–100 (2 a click), a setting for the whole unit (not saved with patches). It dirties HOME's scene only; the panel pages stay clean and readable, and it never changes the sound.

Dial Stage What happens on HOME
0–15 CLEAN nothing
16–65 ITCH the dog's outline boils, more as you turn it up
66–90 SCRATCH + bands of the painting shear sideways
91–100 MANGE + the fence's text scrambles, mustard blotches appear on the painting, the boil stutters

Turn it down and the rot clears. The beam and the bottom bar are never touched. Every flicker is small and slow (under 7 times a second, never the whole screen at once).

1.9 Saving: THE POUND and THE PACK

  • Slots 1–32 (THE POUND) are the factory patches and are locked. You can tweak them as much as you like while playing; you just can't save over them. A firmware update brings their latest voicing.
  • To save: tap SAVE. The header shows the slot it will save into and what is there now. On a POUND patch that is the first free slot from 33; on a PACK patch, the slot you are on. Turn PRESETS to choose another slot (it stays inside 33–99). Tap SAVE again to save: the header says SAVED and you are now on that slot. Do nothing for 3 seconds and SAVE lets go without saving.
  • Saves keep their scene (1.8) and survive a power-cycle.
  • SAVE armed + press SELECT = randomise: a new random sound instead of saving.
  • From v0.1 / v0.2: a save made over 1–32 before the lock existed moves to the first free PACK slot at the first power-on. If THE PACK is full, it stays where it was, unread.

1.10 Installing, leaving and coming back

  • Install from Chrome or Edge with the installer page (vincentzsk-prod.github.io/dog5/install/), over USB. It works from the stock firmware and from another custom firmware. Keep the installer tab in front until it says Done: in a background tab Chrome slows the page down, and the unit gives up waiting (it shows UPDATE FAILED). If an install is cut off, the unit stays in update mode and the page offers Resume.
  • Leave and come back: another firmware (from the Firmware Hub, say) installs over DØG-5 the usual way, and DØG-5 installs back over it. Tested on the unit 20–21 Nov.
  • Your saves belong to DØG-5. It reads only its own saved patches. Another firmware's saves don't show up here, and saving in DØG-5 can write over them. Other firmwares may treat DØG-5's saves the same way. Back up first (M-Flasher's BACKUP FULL FLASH) if anything on the unit matters to you.
  • Back to stock: M-Flasher's DOWNLOAD MODE works from DØG-5, and RESTORE FULL FLASH with your stock backup puts the original firmware back. Tested on the unit 21 Nov.
  • The flash chip. DØG-5 was built and tested on an FM-1 with the older Puya P25Q80 flash chip (0x856014). Newer units with the UC25HQ80 (0xB36014) are accepted by the update loader, but DØG-5 has never been installed or played on one. M-Flasher's Device Info shows which chip yours has.

PART 2 — THE VOICING DICTIONARY

The shared language for describing and shaping tone. Each term gives the plain meaning and the controls that move it, so a direction like "fatter and nastier, but less wet" has one agreed reading. This is the contract for the voicing process and the vocabulary the patch descriptions are written in.

Body & weight

  • Fat / thick — more body and width. More: OSC 2 LEVEL up, slight DETUNE, UNISON or DUAL mode, sub/low register, both oscillators on. The DØG-5 method: start fat, then drive — never a thin source pushed loud. (Measured on stacked-saw patches: once the oscillators are stacked, rebalancing levels or filter barely changes the spectrum; what changes the feel is stack width (DETUNE), level and harmonic density (filter DRIVE).)
  • Thin / hollow — narrow, reedy, little body. More: single oscillator, pulse with narrow PW, higher register, less detune. (Diagnosis tip: very low notes put most of their energy under about 60 Hz, which small speakers and many PAs don't reproduce — "thin" on a low patch is often the 60–400 Hz band, not the sub.)
  • Sub-heavy / deep — weight in the low end. More: low octave, OSC 2 down an octave, low cutoff with the filter drive doing the work (bass-comp). (At the very bottom, A0–A1, an octave-down oscillator is below audible range — it costs headroom without adding weight.)
  • Full vs empty — how much of the spectrum is filled. Fuller = both oscs + noise; emptier = one osc, no noise.
  • Muddy (added 5 Nov, from 05 ZEAROX round 1; extended 6 Nov) — energy piled up in 150–400 Hz with almost nothing above 1.2 kHz, and a long tail: a smear, not a punch. Cause found: a saw wave through a 24 dB low-pass at a low cutoff, plus GROWL's compression lengthening the tail. Cure: square/pulse oscillators, an open 12 dB filter, no GROWL, a short decay. Diagnose with the 150–400 Hz share against the 1.2 kHz+ share ("MUD ratio") in time windows. Scale (6 Nov, from Chapter II): 10 A 2.5; 12 C 12.3 (tail 10 / 15 / 77); a "medium muddy" target is about 10–40 on the note, tail windows no worse than about 80; 13 (final) 315 with tails over 1000 — very muddy, chosen by ear; 16 D 133 (almost nothing above 1.2 kHz). A soft, triangle-like tone is not "medium muddy" by this ratio on its own (245 with the second oscillator off in 13's round 1); the ratio is a diagnostic, and the owner's ear decides.
  • Blank slate / init (added 12 Nov, from 32 Init bruv?) — a plain starting voice with nothing added: no modulation, no echo, no spring, no tape, no drive. In this bank it is the engine's own default program (two saws 4.7 cents apart through a 24 dB low-pass at CUTOFF 80, RESO 20), not a single raw saw with an open filter (the saw's harmonics follow 1/n only with OSC 2 off, CUTOFF 127, RESO 0 and flat envelopes, which is a separate "raw saw" render kept for later).

Brightness & tone

  • Bright — more high end, more presence. More: CUTOFF up (HOME/FILTER), ENV AMT up, less SPRING DAMP, less BBD TONE roll-off, less TAPE head-loss.
  • Presence (added 4 Nov, from 30 THE DØG) — the patch sits forward and fills the room without simply being louder or fuzzier. More: a wider stack (DETUNE), a touch more CUTOFF, per-voice filter DRIVE (warms without compressing), and — for a flagship only — sitting at the top of the loudness tolerance.
  • Dark / murky — rolled-off top. More: CUTOFF down, more DAMP, more TONE roll-off on the delay.
  • Distant / "at the bottom of a well" (added 4 Nov, from 09 Skeenhead) — the note's body vanishes and only the effects remain, so note and effect feel like two separate events. Cause found: the filter's cutoff resting below the played notes (a resonant plop closing under them), leaving a dark hum with no top, while the spring stays bright. Cure: raise the CUTOFF floor and the FILTER sustain so the filter rests above the notes; check the effect level relative to the dry note per time window (a single average hides it).
  • Warm — soft top without going dull; gentle saturation. More: a little per-voice filter DRIVE (MIXER page, knob 4), LP filter, modest cutoff. (Not "a touch of GROWL": GROWL does almost nothing below about 28.)
  • Harsh / brittle / piercing — aggressive, possibly fatiguing highs. More: high RESO near self-osc, high cutoff, hard sync, GROWL with high BIAS. Usually a thing to dial back.
  • Nasal / honky — mid-forward, vowel-like. More: band-pass filter type, narrow PW, or TYPE SEM with MORPH toward notch.
  • Zap (added 5 Nov, from 08 Wire Bite) — a burst of top end at the strike, like biting a live wire. More: narrow pulses, resonance, a fast filter envelope. Limit: a generally brighter cutoff shrinks the measured burst (the body is already bright), so "zappier" and "brighter" pull against each other.
  • Soft / triangle-like (added 6 Nov, from 11, 16 D and 13) — there is no triangle or sine oscillator. The nearest is a narrow pulse (about 25%) through a key-tracking 12 dB low-pass: harmonics 3 / 5 / 7 read about −17 / −27 / −37 dB against an ideal triangle's −19 / −28 / −34. It is dark (centroid about 600 Hz, almost nothing above 1.2 kHz) and the ratio calls it muddy. An octave-up copy of the pulse brings the ratio down (13's round 1). It is a triangle-like stack, not a sine.
  • Chime (band-limited) (added 12 Nov, from 29 i scream) — a bright struck ping inside a narrow band, like a small horn speaker. How it is built: a 12 dB band-pass at CUTOFF 77, RESO 105, KEY TRK 0 (peaks at 1099 Hz, −3 dB width 898–1345 Hz; 0.4% of its energy under 400 Hz and 4.1% above 4 kHz, measured with white noise), a pulse at 50% for OSC 1, and a second oscillator +15 semitones with X-MOD 25 and ENV>O2 76 for the zing at the strike. Limit: the +15 semitone partial is faint at the top of the keybed (−34 dB at C#6, −18 dB at C#5).

Dirt & aggression

  • Clean — no added grit. GROWL at 0 (a true bypass).
  • Driven / pushed — console-into-the-red warmth to crunch. More: filter DRIVE for the gentle route (adds harmonics without squashing dynamics; it sits before the filter, so the filter takes some of the edge back); GROWL for the big step (inert up to about 28, compresses past about 40, fuzzy by about 70); BIAS (inside GROWL) adds peaks and even-harmonic buzz. (12 Nov, from 26 BSyncA: GROWL also darkens a sync strike — the centroid over the first 50 ms is 2662 Hz with GROWL 44 against 4165 Hz with no drive — so the rip's brightness trades against the drive.)
  • Nasty / gnarly / blown — full aggression. More: GROWL high, resonant filter, hard-chop gate. The Chapter I register.
  • Fuzzy / voltage-starved — gated, spitting fuzz like a dying battery. More: GROWL maxed into a thick source, cutoff open, fast gate. (Measured on 06: held-note crest factor falls 5.8 dB at GROWL 0, 3.7 at 55, 2.3 at 76, 1.5 at 100. Sustain comes from the amp envelope, not from GROWL. TONE is the audible one of GROWL's secondary controls; BIAS barely changes the peak.)
  • Pixelated / black-and-white (added 5 Nov, from 05 ZEAROX) — a hard two-level wave, like a photocopy reduced to pure black and white: harsh, glitchy, not smeared. More: pulse/square oscillators only, a 12 dB filter held open, no GROWL, no tape. Measured as the share of samples within 10% of the rail: pulse waves 54% against 24% for saws; 05's final patch reads 94–98%.
  • Spitting / biting — nervous, articulate attack grit. More: VINTAGE slop + a snappy gate + drive; comes from drive biting a thick source, not a thin one.
  • Gritty / crunchy — midway dirt. GROWL in the 30–40 zone, or heavy filter DRIVE. (12 Nov, from 28 round 2: on an FM bell the top grit was the FM itself — X-MOD 64 → 32 lowered the 2–10 kHz roughness, spectral flatness at A4 −16.9 → −25.4 dB — not CHEW, GROWL or drive. The share of energy above 4 kHz did not move: that is the saw's harmonics through an open filter at the strike, which suggests it moves with CUTOFF and the filter envelope.)
  • Dust (trace noise) (added 7 Nov, from 23 Crypt Dust) — noise present only as a faint dust under the tone. Measured: the owner heard full-level noise (NOISE 127) as drowning a thin pulse even though the noise was only about 6 dB under the pulse by level, because it fills the spectrum between the pulse's harmonics; the final patch has the noise 24.4 dB under the pulse (NOISE 43; the NOISE knob is a square law: 43 against 127 is −18.8 dB). Removing the noise lowered the centroid by about 1.2 kHz and the 4 kHz+ share from 2.5% to 0.7%.

Movement & instability

  • Tight / stable — locked, in tune, steady. More: VINTAGE/slop low, no LFO pitch, SYNC phase.
  • Slop — the DØG-5 instability macro: per-voice tuning drift and wander. Low = solid, mid = seasick, high = dying tape motor. Rideable live on ALGORITHM. (Measured: the patch's own VINTAGE is gentle — at 127 each voice wanders only about 6 cents. The dying-tape-motor territory comes mostly from the ALGORITHM ride, which multiplies the patch's own slop: about 5.6× at VINTAGE 55, 3.8× at 90 and 3.0× at 127.)
  • Seasick / woozy — slow pitch sway that unsettles. More: VINTAGE up, slow LFO→PITCH, slow TAPE wow.
  • Warped / chewed — tape-style wobble and dropouts. More: CHEW up (wow/flutter/dropouts). Costs noticeably more CPU (about +770–784 host instr/sample at high CHEW; a Titanic variant with CHEW measured 2371 vs 1594). (Measured on 05 round 1: CHEW at maximum barely changed level, crest or click — it mostly smeared the top end. Measured on 13 round 1: the deck's wobble is about 2.3 / 4.1 / 6.2 / 6.5 cents s.d. at CHEW 40 / 70 / 100 / 127, slow wow only (0.3–0.5 Hz), and it added hiss that lifts the centroid. The owner heard the wobble as "killing the overall tone" and dropped it, so CHEW 0 on 13. On 29 the owner also took the tape off after hearing it: CHEW 65 cost 2647 host instr/sample against 1863 with CHEW 0.)
  • Melt (added 7 Nov, from 22 Melting Orb) — the filter closing and the pitch sinking together over a few seconds while the key is held. How: a rising filter envelope (FA 118, 4.96 s nominal) with a negative ENV AMT, plus ENV>O2 below centre (it bends OSC 2 only, from the filter envelope: (value − 64) × 24/63 semitones at the top; value 46 = −6.86 st). Measured: −678 cents final, 90% of the fall at 4.0 s, centroid 1323 → 204 Hz. Limit: on key-up the filter envelope releases and the melt partly runs backwards through the fade.
  • Wobble — regular pitch or PWM movement. More: LFO→PITCH or LFO→PWM, moderate rate. (PWM: the pulse width sweep runs at the LFO rate. A sweep that crosses 50% sounds like it doubles its rate, because a pulse and its mirror width sound alike; keep the sweep on one side of 50%, or only just across it. Through a murky low-pass the PWM movement is a ceiling of about 10 dB in the 150–400 Hz band whatever the depth or cutoff (12 Kelp Tangle); a faster, wider sweep or more per-voice DRIVE trades level swing for band depth.)
  • Beating / shimmer (added 6 Nov, from 10 and 13) — two oscillators a few cents apart drift in and out of phase, so the low-mid band swells and dips about once a second without any LFO. Measured: 10 A (a pulse pair with one 85% pulse nearly the inverse of the 16% one, +9.4 cents) swings its A3 band 17.9 dB at 1.01 Hz; 13 (pair +7.0 cents) moves the 150–400 Hz band 13.6–13.8 dB at 0.9 Hz on one voice (6.2 dB on the held chord). Removing the detune (OSC 2 FINE 64) takes it to 0.3 dB; removing the PWM LFO leaves it. Slow PWM sweeps are a different movement, mostly in the 400–1.2k band (3.9 dB on 13's original).
  • Drifting — slow, unrepeating wander (not a steady LFO). More: VINTAGE slop, a slow smooth-random LFO→PITCH (08 Wire Bite: ±19 cents at 0.28 Hz). (There is no Poly-Mod control: X-MOD is OSC 2 → OSC 1 FM; checked again 6 Nov for 18.) Wander (added 7 Nov, from 18 Roto-scopo) — the Poly-Mod substitute: the one shared smooth-random LFO (0.11 Hz) on the FILTER (±23.9 st) over a resonant low-pass, plus VINTAGE slop 127. Measured on A1: the centroid ranges 316–708 Hz (14 st); the level moves only about 1 dB. The wander is common to all voices and cannot follow OSC 2.
  • Glitchy (added 5 Nov, from 07 Tape Splice) — nervous, broken, unreliable pitch and level. More: a fast random or sample-and-hold LFO to PITCH (5–21 Hz, ±19 cents up to several semitones), tape dropouts (CHEW high with DROPS up). (Measured: the random pitch LFO carries the pitch jitter; tape carries the dips; X-MOD adds sidebands and low-end energy but does not move the measured pitch.)
  • Chorus (clear, wide) (added 6 Nov, from 10 round 1) — the engine has no chorus effect. A chorus is built from a DUAL pair (SPREAD 127) with a slow TRI pitch LFO in PHASE SPREAD, so the two voices of each note sit 45° apart in the LFO and their pitch difference swings. Measured on 10 B: ±19 cents at 0.72 Hz, L/R correlation 0.48 (0.78 without), band beating 29 dB. It costs about +490 host instr/sample over POLY (10 B 2294). A short BBD delay cannot be a chorus, because its time has no LFO.
  • Leslie-style (rotary) (added 6 Nov) — vibrato plus tremolo from the one LFO routed to PITCH and AMP in PHASE FREE. Only an in-phase approximation: a real rotor's pitch and level are 90° apart and the engine has one LFO. With SPREAD the tremolo cancels in the sum (2.2 dB at AMP 45 with SPREAD, 2.9 FREE, 3.9 SYNC on a held chord).

Space & wetness

  • Dry — no effects tail. The chain mixes/macros at 0.
  • Wet / washed / drenched — lots of tail. More: SPRING DRAIN up, BBD MIX + FEEDBK up.
  • Wash (washy, not punchy) (added 6 Nov, from 16 Tidal Pull) — a chord that blooms in, trails into its own echo and spring and moves. More: a medium amp attack (AA 82 reads 17 / 93 / 219 ms to 10 / 50 / 90%; the envelope's nominal time is 1.3–1.4× its time to 90%), a slow TRI pitch LFO (±19 cents), a spread of detuned voices, echo at about 337 ms with FEEDBK 78 and MIX 110, DRAIN 45 SIZE 90. Keep the echo audibly above the spring (16 D: first repeat −8.6 dB re the note, 7.7 dB above the spring).
  • Hover (added 7 Nov, from 19 Micro-mist and 24 Fugue State) — a chord that keeps hanging in the air on its own echo and spring after the key is up. More: echo FEEDBK near 100 or above with ALLEY 100–144 ms, a large spring (SIZE 100–110), a slow release. Measured: 19 D falls 20 / 40 / 60 dB in 1596 / 4132 / 5788 ms after a 10 s chord; 24 C in 1648 / 3520 / 4624 ms. Limits: it is a decaying hover, not a freeze (no freeze, reverse or pitch-shifted repeats exist); FEEDBK 122 on 24 would peak at −2.1 dBFS, 127 clips.
  • Slap / slapback — one short, loud echo. More: ALLEY short (free ms), FEEDBK low, MIX up. (Measured on a bass: the echo is a faithful copy of the note, so ALLEY TONE does nothing audible there — the crispness has to live in the note. The loudest slap the engine can make is MIX 127, about 6 dB under the note's peak.)
  • Springy / boingy — the spring-reverb chirp and flutter. More: DRAIN up, SIZE up; the Chapter II sound. (Watch "tubby" — too much low-mid in the tail.) (Measured: DRAIN is audible on bass, not absent — the tank's high-pass is one-pole, −9 dB at 55 Hz. At DRAIN 60 the return is about −5 dB re dry on Titanic and −9.7 dB on a bass with most energy below 150 Hz. The spring sits after the echo and rings the repeats; it is fed the filtered voice, so a murky patch gets a murky tail.)
  • Roomy vs close — amount and length of ambience (SIZE/PRE-DLY vs dry). (PRE-DLY 4 is only about 1 ms.)
  • Wet return, measured per window — for a patch with a slight wetness (01 Red Pill) the effect level is read relative to the dry note in 0–20 / 20–100 / 100–250 ms windows, never as an average.

Envelope, attack & dynamics

  • Snappy / punchy — fast attack, quick decay, immediate. More: AMP/FILTER ATTACK low, DECAY short. (Where the punch lives: often in the filter envelope opening and closing — the brightness falling from attack to body — rather than in the amp level. A fast amp pluck can't reach the bank level on its own. A heavily clipped sound (06, 05) has almost no level spike at the strike; its punch is the quick rise.)
  • Plucky — percussive, fast decay, little sustain. More: short DECAY, low SUSTAIN, filter env.
  • Gated (as opposed to plucky) (added 4 Nov, from 11 Slapback Strut) — zero decay: the note starts at once, holds its body for the length of the key, and stops in about a millisecond. Note: removing a pluck's decay can make the note duller, because the pluck's initial tap carried the top end; to end up bright, raise the cutoff and narrow the pulse.
  • Soft / slow / swelling — gentle fade-in. More: ATTACK up, SUSTAIN high.
  • Bloom (added 4 Nov, from 21 Cowl Shadow) — a slow filter-envelope swell that opens while the key is held: dark and soft at first, then wide and bright. It needs the key (or a sustain pedal) held for its full length; released early it never opens, it just fades. Short stabs on a bloom patch are far quieter than the bloomed state.
  • Sustained / drone — holds indefinitely. More: high SUSTAIN, long RELEASE. Live: press REC (HOLD) with the arpeggiator off and the held notes keep ringing until you press REC again, STOP, or send a MIDI panic (see 1.1).
  • Choppy / gated / staccato — hard on/off, dead silence between notes. More: fast RELEASE (hard-chop VCA), LFO→VCA square tremolo. The house dynamic — the impact of the noise comes from the silence after it.
  • Chop / strobe (added 5 Nov, from 15 Trem Chop) — a hard on/off tremolo from a SQUARE LFO routed to AMP at full depth: about 43–45 dB between the on and off parts at AMP 127 (17 dB at 110, 13.5 at 100, 9 at 80). Rate is the RATE knob alone: 0.05 × 600^(RATE/127) Hz, steps of about 5%. Limits: no tempo sync; PHASE SYNC restarts the chop on each detached note (so every note starts ON), FREE phase is unpredictable live; VINTAGE does not make the chop edges waver — only PHASE SPREAD on a DUAL pair does (the two voices chop an eighth of a cycle apart).
  • Sputter (added 4 Nov, from Half-Life) — the tail doesn't fade, it breaks into a few ragged stutters as the note dies. Distinct from tremolo: the body is clean and only the tail chops. More: LFO SHAPE SQUARE around 20 Hz routed to AMP at full depth, with LFO DELAY around 110 ms so the chop fades in after the attack. Limit: the chop follows how long the note has been sounding, not the key coming up, so it works on short notes (roughly 150–180 ms); a longer held note spits all the way through.
  • Rip (added 4 Nov, from V-Sync) — the hard-sync sweep: the synced oscillator's pitch tears down across the note. Limit: in MONO and UNISON, a note struck while another is held slides in and does not re-fire the envelopes, so the rip fires on detached notes only.
  • Crash / burst (added 6 Nov, from 14 Reef Break) — a noise strike that rings out like a cymbal over a square sub. Recipe that worked: NOISE 127 over a square sub (noise 3–6 dB above it in the first 100 ms), a 12 dB HIGH-pass at CUTOFF 100 with ENV AMT 0 (the cutoff starts about 97 semitones low at the strike, under the sub, and climbs back as the filter envelope falls, FD 100), AD = AR = 97 for the ring-out. The bands then fall lowest first and the top rings longest, as a cymbal does; a closing low-pass does the reverse. Attack options measured at 10 / 50 / 90%: 0 / 0.2 / 8.5 ms (near-instant), 2.2 / 8.7 / 27.2 ms (a quick swell, peak at 27 ms; chosen in round 1), 1.2 / 7.2 / 8.7 ms. v0.2 (18 Nov, by ear: the strike was too harsh coming in): 14 now uses a 299 ms attack on both envelopes (FILTER ENV and AMP ENV ATTACK 82), so the crash swells in; every band peaks about 235–276 ms in, the bands still fall lowest first and the top still rings longest. Limits: no inharmonic cymbal partials (noise only); noise and sub share one filter and one amp envelope, so the sub leaves early only through the high-pass; a chord of three noise voices stacks and peaks near the rail.

Struck & ringing (added 12 Nov, from 28 Arr 2 Dee 2 and 29 i scream)

  • Bell (struck) — a sustained, struck tone with inharmonic partials that ring on after the key is up. How it is built (28): two saws, OSC 2 +15 semitones (a ratio of 2.38) feeding OSC 1 by X-MOD 32, a long amp release (AR 116), a slow shimmer. Measured: the five classical bell partials are present at fixed ratios (hum 0.5, prime 1, tierce 1.2, quint 1.5, nominal 2); the key you press is the hum and the prime sits an octave above it. Limits: ENV>O2 ±10 breaks the bell (the tierce falls from −10 dB to about −47 dB); one saw modulating another is not a DX7-style operator stack.
  • Ring — how long a struck note takes to die, read as the milliseconds to fall 6 / 12 / 20 / 30 / 40 dB after the peak. Measured: 28 at A4 915 / 1962 / 3094 / 4700 / 5963 ms; a note released at 400 ms rings on and falls 20 dB in 3012 ms. Not "dreamy" or "healthy" — those are the owner's words.
  • Crystalline (not carried) — a tail whose upper partials outlast the body. The engine has no per-partial envelope, so it cannot be built here; the share of energy above 4 kHz at A4 falls from 4.0% in the first 20 ms to 0.4% at 1–2 s.

DØG-5 house words

  • Blown console — the overall Chapter I aesthetic: fat sources shoved through drive until they tear.
  • The thesis — the pure DØG-5 move: a thick source + slop + hard-chop gate (see Half-Life).
  • The Monologue — the reference point for a patch that "sits under" a spoken/sung vocal in the mix.

PART 2B — TALKING IN NUMBERS (direct parameter moves)

Alongside the character words above, voicing uses plain synth-talk — direct moves on named controls ("cutoff down 10%", "more delay feedback", "LFO rate up a touch"). These rules keep that unambiguous.

The percent convention. A percentage means percent of the control's full range — not of its current value, and not of the number on screen. Most DØG-5 parameters run 0–127, so:

  • "−10%" / "down 10%" = subtract ~13 (10% of 127).
  • "set to 40%" = ~51.
  • rough sizes: a touch ≈ 5% (~6 steps) · a bit ≈ 10% · a lot ≈ 25–30%.

Relative vs absolute are both fine — "more feedback" / "+10%" (from where it is) or "set cutoff to 40%" / "cutoff at 51" (a target). Say which when it matters; if unsaid, "more/less/up/down" is relative and "set to / at" is absolute.

The echo rule. Every change the session makes is reported in concrete before→after: "CUTOFF 80 → 67 (−10%)." So a misread shows up in the notes, not just the sound — you catch it in the echo and correct it there, which is faster than another render.

Controls that aren't a plain 0–127 percent — talk in their own units when that's easier:

Control Native unit How to say it
BBD DELAY time (ALLEY) free ms, 10–740 "delay to 120 ms", or % of range
OSC 2 SEMI semitones, −24…+24 "OSC 2 up a fifth" (+7), "down an octave" (−12)
ENV AMT, FINE, ENV>O2 bipolar, centre 64 "+/−" from centre
OCT, BEND octaves / semitones in their own units
WAVE, MODE, FILTER TYPE, SYNC, LFO SHAPE/PHASE named settings (switches) by name ("pulse", "UNISON", "band-pass")
TEMPO BPM in BPM
FLEAS 0–100 (a screen setting, never the sound) by stage ("ITCH", "MANGE") or number

Everything else is the straight 0–127 percent. (Level knobs such as OSC LEVEL and VOLUME follow a square law, so a small number change is a larger loudness change than it looks.)

Phrasebook — common synth-talk → the DØG-5 control it moves (so a generic instruction lands on the right page/knob):

  • "open / close the filter" → CUTOFF (HOME K1, or the FILTER page)
  • "more resonance / more Q" → RESO
  • "more / less attack · decay · sustain · release" → the AMP ENV or FILTER ENV page (say which)
  • "more filter envelope / more sweep" → ENV AMT
  • "speed up / slow the wobble" → LFO RATE (the SELECT dial on HOME, or the LFO page; and check LFO DEST is on PITCH / PWM / FILTER)
  • "more warmth / a bit more drive" → per-voice DRIVE (MIXER page, knob 4); "more dirt / grit / fuzz" → GROWL (DRIVE page, meaningful from about 30); "more buzz / edge" → BIAS
  • "more delay feedback / more repeats" → FEEDBK (BBD page); "longer / shorter delay" → ALLEY
  • "wetter / more reverb" → DRAIN (SPRING page); "bigger tail" → SIZE
  • "more tape / more wobble / more lo-fi" → CHEW (TAPE page)
  • "detune / thicken / wider" → DETUNE (VOICE page) or OSC 2 FINE
  • "more voices / fatter stack" → MODE + VOICES (UNISON), or the POLY count
  • "how hard is it working / am I near the limit" → GLO once, the CPU reading at the top of GLOBAL (see 1.6)
  • "dirtier screen / cleaner screen" → FLEAS (GLOBAL knob 2; see 1.8)

PART 3 — THE 32 PATCHES

Four chapters of eight. Each chapter is a scene on HOME (the painting the dog stands in, Manual 1.8) with its own accent colour, and a sonic character. Entries marked VOICED are the approved, player-facing description of the finished patch (with gear inspirations in Part 4). Factory patches 1–32 = THE POUND (write-locked: you can play and change them, and a save goes to THE PACK, 33–99).

All 32 are voiced: Chapters I, II, III and IV are complete. (This includes the minimum-gig set.) The patches were voiced on a host renderer and approved by ear; on 12 Nov 2026 Vincent installed the firmware on his FM-1 and reported that all 32 sound distinct and on brand (his words, not measured). Numbers in the entries below are host measurements unless an entry says otherwise. Real-device CPU readings are in DOG-5-device-test-1.md.

CHAPTER I — JALOPY

Egg punk & garage psych. On screen: the Jalopy scene, accent Sun Yellow. Fat sources through a blown console.

  • 01 Red Pill — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant C of Batch 3A).
  • What it sounds like: A nervous, spitting bass made to sit under a vocal. Two fat saws, stacked and held steady, push through a resonant filter that snaps at the start of every note, driven hard enough to be gritty and warm without getting piercing. It is nearly dry: a quick slap and a small spring sit behind each note as an afterthought, lifting it a little and never coming near the note's own loudness.
  • Sound design notes: Low. It was voiced on a riff from A1 up to A2 and on sixteenth-note bursts; other registers are untested. About half of the energy of the low riff is the A1 fundamental, under 60 Hz, so on a small speaker it is the harmonics from about 100 Hz up that carry it. Short detached notes (80–150 ms) are home: the filter snap gives the spit. It is MONO, so legato doesn't re-fire the snap — play it detached; a chord plays one note (the last). The wet is measured: in the loudest of three isolated notes it sits 43.6 / 25.0 / 16.5 dB under the dry note in the 0–20 / 20–100 / 100–250 ms windows, with a short wet tail of about half a second after key-up. Part of the grit is a GROWL step, so it costs more CPU than a plain bass (about 1640 host instr/sample worst case). Slot 1 is the boot patch. Tricks (SLOBBER, SEQ held, kill switch, CHEW) are untested on it.
  • 02 Cement Grind — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant D of Batch 3A).
  • What it sounds like: A low-mid grinder built from two fat pulse waves whose widths sweep quickly, so every note shudders and churns on purpose: a clear, fast pulse-width wobble, not a shimmer. The filter bites, it is pushed into a moderate crunch, and each note starts with a little skid and a snap. Thick, dry, and it hits hard.
  • Sound design notes: A2 up to E3 with G2 (the riff it was voiced on), in notes of about 400 ms, long enough for the wobble to swing two or three times inside a note; other registers are untested. The wobble runs at about 11.5 Hz; on a held A2 it moves the 150–400 Hz band by about 12 dB and the overall level by about 4 dB, and each detached note restarts it. One LFO does both jobs: the pulse-width sweep and a filter wobble run at the same rate; the original slow filter wobble is gone. It is MONO — legato doesn't re-fire the envelopes; play it detached. A chord plays one note. The note stops at once. Don't push the wobble depth much further (the sweep already just crosses 50% at the top of each swing). Light on CPU (about 298 host instr/sample). Tricks untested.
  • 03 Half-Life — VOICED (4 Nov 2026, approved as is). The flagship of the unstable, chopped side; the DØG-5 thesis in one patch.
  • What it sounds like: Fat, slop-heavy dual saws with a sub-octave underneath: seasick, never quite in tune with itself, and thick without going murky. Short notes are chopped stone-dead by the gate, and the tail doesn't fade, it sputters — a few ragged stutters as the note dies. A raw, dry, engine-only sound with no effects on it: the drift and the chop are the whole point.
  • Sound design notes: Low to low-mid register — roots and fifths from about A1 to A3, with fifth-and-octave power chords as home ground. Play it staccato: short notes of roughly 150–180 ms give a hard clean body and a sputtering tail. Held pads and sustained leads are the wrong job; use it for riffs and stabs. Keep chords to three notes (every note is two voices; a fourth note steals voices from earlier ones). Best trick: ride the ALGORITHM (SLOBBER) up to push it from seasick to dying tape motor. Tape Stop (SEQ held) makes a good riff ending; the kill switch (HEEL) stops the sound and the sputter dead. The Psych Chain macros are off on purpose; the dry chop is the sound, and a wash of ALLEY or DRAIN will bury the sputter (untested with this patch).
  • 04 V-Sync — VOICED (4–5 Nov 2026, approved as is).
  • What it sounds like: A tearing hard-sync lead: the pitch of the synced oscillator rips down on every note, nasal and biting, with a plain saw underneath for body. A pair of voices a few cents apart makes it fat enough to cut through a drum machine, and the note stops dead when you let go, with only a faint quick slap behind it. Raw on purpose: that is where the rip lives.
  • Sound design notes: Mid register, roughly A3–A4. One note at a time. Play it staccato: in MONO and UNISON a note struck while another is held slides in and doesn't re-fire the envelopes, so the sweep fires on detached notes only (a legato run glides and rips once, on its first note). The voice stops dead on release; a faint 1/16 slap follows each note (echo MIX to 0 for a literal dead stop). Tricks: ALGORITHM pulls the two voices apart, kill switch kills the slap too, Tape Stop dives a held note — all untested on this patch. A wash of DRAIN will blur the rip.
  • 05 ZEAROX — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant D of round 2 — round 1 was rejected).
  • What it sounds like: A kick substitute made of one hard square wave, built toward a pixelated, gritty, blown-out sound like a photocopy reduced to pure black and white. The pitch drops fast over the first 11 ms, and a random stepped pitch LFO moves it to a new value every 47 ms or so, so a 150 ms hit gets about three random pitch steps of up to ±4.7 semitones (a longer note gets more). The wave stays almost entirely at its two extreme levels, there is no attack, and the hit stops quickly. Dry: no tape, no drive, no echo, no spring.
  • Sound design notes: Low hits on A0, A1 and A2 (and four-in-a-bar A1 at 120 BPM); other registers are untested. It is MONO — legato doesn't re-fire the envelopes; play it detached. The kick is mostly the quick pitch drop; there is no click spike. A0 is still mostly sub (81% of its energy under 60 Hz after the first 20 ms): a 27.5 Hz square is inaudible on a small speaker whatever is done. VOLUME is 123 of 127, so there is almost no knob headroom above the bank reference. It is the lightest patch of its batch (about 1337 host instr/sample). The random LFO is free-running, so it is not bit-comparable from the boot patch. Tricks untested.
  • 06 zzuFuzz — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant C of Batch 3A). The fuzz weapon.
  • What it sounds like: A huge, thick wall. Two fat saws on every voice are pushed hard into the drive until the sound is flat and relentless, and it simply does not die while you hold the key. The strike is quick (about 2 ms), the filter and its resonance are wide open, and when you let go there is a short tail of about a third of a second rather than a ring. Completely dry: no echo, no spring. A power chord stays whole.
  • Sound design notes: A low A1 up to power chords around A2–E3–A3, held or stabbed; other registers are untested. The held note's level falls by nothing over three seconds, and its peak-to-RMS ratio is 1.7 dB (a square wave is 0). It is POLY with 6 voices, so every key re-fires the envelopes and a three-note chord plays whole. The strike's punch is the quick rise, not a level spike (+0.3 dB over the plateau): more punch would mean less wall. It reads about 2 dB hotter than the bank on the standard stabs phrase (the cause was not isolated), and VOLUME changes how a note from silence starts, because GROWL's loudness trim reads the output stage: set VOLUME first. Honest limit: it was built toward a Fuzz War-class wall from descriptions and approved by ear; nothing says it matches a real pedal, and the starved, gating sputter of the voltage-starved fuzzes is not in it. The GROWL costs about +595 host instr/sample (about 1414 worst case).
  • 07 Tape Splice — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant B of Batch 3B).
  • What it sounds like: A fat square with a wobble in its pitch, chopped short. Two square waves a hair apart, one frequency-modulating the other so the tone carries extra energy below the note, and a random pitch wobble (about 9.6 cents standard deviation, the LFO depth up to ±19 cents). Notes stop quickly when you let go, and a tape stage on the end delays each note by a couple of milliseconds. Dry.
  • Sound design notes: Staccato notes from A2 up to G3 (twelve 60 ms notes) and a held A2; other registers are untested. It is MONO — legato doesn't re-fire the envelopes; play it detached. A chord plays one note. The pitch wobble comes from the random LFO; X-MOD adds sidebands and low-end energy but does not move the measured pitch. No dropouts were measured at the shipped tape setting (a harsher setting, CHEW 127, produces them and costs more). About 2177 host instr/sample worst case, about 770 of it the tape. Tricks untested.
  • 08 Wire Bite — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant D of Batch 3A).
  • What it sounds like: An anxious, thick drone that bites, like touching a live wire. Six stacked pulse waves in the high register with a second layer an octave and a fifth above, through a resonant filter that zaps at the start of every note. Fat and bright (medium to high), and it never sits still: the voices wander on their own and the whole stack leans and jitters in pitch. Dry, and each note is chopped off the moment you let go.
  • Sound design notes: High: a held A4, eight 110 ms bites (E5, A4, C5, D5) and a held A3; low notes and other registers are untested. It is a UNISON of 6 voices — legato doesn't re-fire the envelopes: a key held while the next goes down slides and the zap doesn't happen again; play it detached. Chords play one note. The drift is measured from the engine's own log: static offsets of −9 to +7 cents between the voices, each wandering 4–6 cents, and a smooth-random pitch LFO leaning the stack up to 19 cents at 0.28 Hz. The measured top-end burst at the strike is small, because the body is so bright; it was approved by ear. A bite is 40 dB down 18 ms after the key goes up. The original's echo and spring were removed (about 1298 host instr/sample). Tricks untested.

CHAPTER II — BEE-TCH

Surf rock & skinhead reggae. On screen: the Bee-tch scene, accent Wave Turquoise. The spring-reverb chapter. All eight patches (09–16) are voiced.

  • 09 Skeenhead — VOICED (4–5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant E of round 2). The reggae off-beat stab.
  • What it sounds like: A tight, plucky square stab with a resonant plop on the front, drenched in spring. The note has a body that holds for as long as you play it; the spring rings on after the note and is the sound of the patch. A wet, springy, boingy reggae stab.
  • Sound design notes: Off-beat two-note stabs of about a tenth of a second, around A3 to C4 (the skank it was voiced on); other registers are untested. The plop is still there but softer than in the first version — the first 20 ms is only a few dB above the body. The filter now rests above the played notes, so the body survives the gate. The spring is the sound: it ships at DRAIN 90, about 6 dB under the dry note over a stab, and is louder than the note in the 100–250 ms after it (natural for a spring), with a tail of about 1.1 s. One oscillator, no LFO, no detune; VINTAGE is the default 30 (no wander was measured, so steadiness isn't claimed). It is a stab patch; held notes were not measured. Tricks (SLOBBER, Tape Stop, kill switch, ALLEY, turning DRAIN down) are untested on it.
  • 10 Atlantic Swell — VOICED (6 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant A of Batch 4A, the starting point unchanged).
  • What it sounds like: A bright pair of narrow pulse waves through a notch filter, played polyphonically, with a spring reverb behind it and nothing else. It has no vibrato, no chorus and no delay (measured). The two pulses beat slowly against each other and the spring rings on after the notes.
  • Sound design notes: Organ chords and short notes: voiced on an A minor triad (A3 C4 E4) held 2.4 s, a 120 ms E4, four 120 ms notes and a D minor triad (D4 F4 A4); other registers are untested. POLY 5. The beating: on the held chord an A3 band swings 17.9 dB at about 1 Hz (no LFO is needed for it; the pulse width LFO, ±2.3 points, is not audible as PWM). Bright: the note-on centroid is 5369 Hz and 23% of the energy is above 1.2 kHz. The spring (DRAIN 40, SIZE 100) is louder than the notes by the last two of four staccato notes (−0.8 / −0.4 dB re each note), so fast playing blurs into the tail. Level −19.0 dBFS RMS on its own phrase at VOLUME 100 (the bank reference is −18.0 ± 1.5). Versions with a chorus, a rotary-speaker tremolo and a heavy echo were rendered (B, C, D, on the Batch 4A listening branch) and are not this patch; they stay a v1.1 candidate. "Cold" and "crisp" were not measured. About 2020 host instr/sample worst case. The first play after power-on differs from a program-load render by about −25 dB (not isolated). Tricks untested.
  • 11 Slapback Strut — VOICED (4–5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant G of round 2). Percussive surf bass — now a gated bass with one loud slap.
  • What it sounds like: A tight, gated surf bass: the note starts at once, holds its body for as long as you hold the key, and stops dead. Behind each note comes one clean, loud echo, a plain copy of the note a moment later, and then nothing. Bright and crisp on top for a bass, sharp and a little biting, and dry otherwise.
  • Sound design notes: Low, A1 to A2 (the surf riff it was voiced on). It is a gated bass, not a pluck — the first version's pluck was traded away for crispness. There is no triangle oscillator, so the sound is a narrow pulse through a key-tracking low-pass, bright enough that its upper harmonics are near a square wave's: sharp and biting, and it may buzz on a very bright amp. The slap is one copy at 80 ms (first repeat about 6 dB under the note's peak, the second much lower) and already at the engine's maximum; the delay's TONE does nothing audible on this bass. Mono — play it detached (legato slides and doesn't re-hit). DRAIN ships at 0; a spring wash behind the slap is untested on this version.
  • 12 Kelp Tangle — VOICED (6 Nov 2026, approved after listening; variant C of Batch 4A, CUTOFF 98).
  • What it sounds like: A pad of pulse waves whose widths are swept slowly and steadily by a single triangle LFO, through a steep low-pass that leaves little in the high register, with a spring tail behind it. The sweep is measurable on held notes; on short notes only a slice of it is heard. No LFO pitch vibrato and no echo are set.
  • Sound design notes: Held chords and notes: voiced on a held A2 (3.2 s), the chord A2 E3 C4 (3 s) and six 150 ms notes; other registers are untested. POLY 5. On a held A2, after the filter, the sweep moves the 150–400 Hz band by 10.1 dB, the 400–1.2k band by 7.6 dB and the level by 5.7 dB; the LFO runs at 1.03 Hz and sweeps the pulse widths 18 to 48% (one side of 50%), restarted on each detached note (PHASE SYNC). On a 150 ms note it is only about 2 dB: the PWM is a held-note effect. Dark: centroid 531 Hz on the held A2, 0.8% of its energy above 1.2 kHz. The spring (DRAIN 55, SIZE 75) comes back at −47 / −13 / −6 dB re the dry chord in the first 250 ms; the tail is 60 dB down about 1.4 s after the chord, and its muddiness ratio is 10 / 15 / 77 in 0–250 / 250–750 / 750–1500 ms (the CUTOFF 86 variant was 29 / 39 / 180). Honest limits: one shared LFO moves both oscillators at one rate and there is no Poly-Mod, so "PWM driven by OSC B" is not possible; the 150–400 Hz depth tops out near 10 dB at any depth or cutoff measured. Level −18.0 dBFS RMS on its own phrase at VOLUME 74. About 2042 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.
  • 13 Ghost Board — VOICED (6 Nov 2026, approved after listening; variant C2 of Batch 4B round 2; the owner expects to dial it further on the FM-1). The brief changed after listening: the original called for a near-sine filtered triangle with maximum tape wow/flutter; the tape wobble was heard as "killing the overall tone" and was dropped, and the near-sine tone was not what was wanted.
  • What it sounds like: A dark pad: a pair of slightly detuned pulse waves, played polyphonically, beating slowly against each other, with a long echo and a heavy spring behind every note. It is the original patch's voice, unchanged, with the pulse-width movement removed and no tape deck. By the dictionary's ratio it is very muddy.
  • Sound design notes: Held chords, a slow line and short notes: voiced on an A minor 7 chord held 2.4 s, four 800 ms notes and six 150 ms notes; other registers are untested. POLY 5. No tape, no tape wobble (a one-voice probe reads 0.0 cents). The movement is the beating between the two oscillators: on one held voice the 150–400 Hz band moves 13.6 dB at 0.9 Hz (6.2 dB on the held chord). Dark and very muddy: note-on centroid 562 Hz, 0.2% of the energy above 1.2 kHz, muddiness ratio 315 (the original measured 108); the tail 1108 / 2198 / 3331 in 0–250 / 250–750 / 750–1500 ms. The echo is 337 ms, FEEDBK 95, MIX 105: on an isolated note the first repeat arrives 337 ms after the note-on at −8.7 dB re the note, 10.3 dB above the spring; the spring (DRAIN 70, SIZE 100) is louder than the chord for its first 250 ms or so. Level −18.0 dBFS RMS on its own phrase at VOLUME 55 (phrase (b) reads −23.4). About 2084 host instr/sample worst case (the tape was 784 of the earlier 2679). A program-load render is bit-identical from the boot patch (the earlier variant with the pulse-width LFO differed by −33 / −41 dB; this suggests the free-running LFO phase, not isolated). Tricks untested.
  • 14 Reef Break — VOICED (6 Nov 2026, round-1 variant C of Batch 4B; the attack changed in v0.2 on 18 Nov, and Vincent approved the new version on the FM-1: "spot on", his words).
  • What it sounds like: A crash made of a burst of noise over a square-wave sub. The noise swells in over a fraction of a second rather than striking at once, the lows fall away first and the top of the noise rings out longest, and a long echo follows each hit. There is no spring and no tape.
  • Sound design notes: One low hit (A1), one mid hit (A2), A1 hits 1000, 600 and 400 ms apart, every gate 300 ms; other registers are untested. POLY 5. Both envelopes have a 299 ms attack (FILTER ENV and AMP ENV ATTACK 82, shown as 299ms): on A1 the hit reaches 10 / 50 / 90% of its peak at 25.2 / 126.2 / 208.0 ms (A2 peaks at 268 ms), and the sub's band peaks 235 ms after the note-on, the top band (4k and up) 255 ms. By band, the time after the note-on at which each has fallen 20 / 40 dB below its own peak: 60–150 Hz 308 / 316 ms; 1.2k–4k 435 / 1120 ms; 4k and up 923 / 1622 ms. The echo is 361 ms, FEEDBK 100, MIX 80: first repeats −13 / −18 / −23 dB re the burst, 8 repeats stay above −40 dB, no clipping. The dry tail rings out in about a second; the echo runs several seconds. Level −18.03 dBFS RMS on its own phrase at VOLUME 116, peak −4.17 dBFS. Three keys struck at once stack three noise voices and peak at −2.82 dBFS (no clipped sample). Limits: no inharmonic cymbal partials; noise and sub share one filter and one amp envelope. About 1857 host instr/sample worst case (measured before the attack change). Tricks untested. (The 6 Nov version struck at once, peaking at 27 ms; Vincent found it too harsh coming in.)
  • 15 Trem Chop — VOICED (5 Nov 2026, approved as is; variant D of Batch 3B; variant B was committed first).
  • What it sounds like: A broken-strobe tremolo: a bright saw chopped on and off by a hard square-shaped LFO, not a gentle sine. Every note is two voices, and the two voices chop an eighth of a cycle apart, so the chop has an off part, a half-level part and a full part instead of a clean on/off. Dry: no echo, no spring, no tape.
  • Sound design notes: A held A3, a six-note riff of 500 ms notes, the chord A3 + E4 + A4 and short 110 ms notes; other registers are untested. It is DUAL with POLY 6, so every note is two voices: a three-note chord uses all six. The chop is 8.10 Hz (the nearest byte to sixteenths at 120 BPM), 44.8 dB between the on and off parts; the held note spends 35% of the time off, 31% at one voice's level and 33% at full. There is no tempo sync with existing controls, so the chop slides against a beat; the card carries the rate table (e.g. 140 BPM sixteenths = RATE 104, 9.42 Hz). The chop edges are steady to 0.18 ms: VINTAGE does not make them waver; the two-voice spread is what makes it sound unsteady. It reads about 2.5 dB hotter than the bank on the stabs phrase, with a peak of −6.2 dBFS (limit −4), and costs about 2375 host instr/sample. LFO PITCH is 0 (the original 8 was inert). Tricks untested.
  • 16 Tidal Pull — VOICED (6 Nov 2026, approved after listening; variant D of Batch 4A, the triangle-like stack).
  • What it sounds like: A stereo chord wash of triangle-like tones (narrow pulses through a low-pass, with an octave-up copy), moved by a slow triangle LFO on pitch. The notes come in gradually, an echo follows each note, and a spring rings behind both. It is a dark patch, not a bright one.
  • Sound design notes: Chords: voiced on A minor 7 (A3 C4 E4 G4) and F major 7 (F3 A3 C4 E4) held 2.0 s, three 400 ms notes and three 100 ms stabs; other registers are untested. POLY 5. It is triangle-like, not a sine, dark and peak-limited: harmonics 3 / 5 / 7 read −17.2 / −27.3 / −36.8 dB against an ideal triangle's −19.1 / −28.0 / −34.2; centroid 595 Hz, 0.5% of the energy above 1.2 kHz, muddiness ratio 133; −19.1 dBFS RMS on its own phrase at VOLUME 76 (1.1 dB under the reference, inside ±1.5; the peak is −4.4). Attack 17 / 93 / 219 ms to 10 / 50 / 90%. The pitch LFO is triangle, 2.30 Hz, ±19 cents (LFO PITCH 16; the original 3 was inert), voices offset by PHASE SPREAD. The echo is 337 ms (ALLEY 104), FEEDBK 78, MIX 110: the first repeat is −8.6 dB re the note and 7.7 dB above the spring. The spring (DRAIN 45, SIZE 90) is −39 / −19 / −14 dB re the note in 0–20 / 20–100 / 100–250 ms. The tail is 20 dB down at 1.2 s and 40 dB down at 2.4 s. Width: the held chord's L/R correlation is 0.70 dry, 0.66 with the echo and spring (an eight-voice DUAL version on variant B read 0.38; not measured here). On this phrase short notes do not reach the level of the held chords (the stabs read 7.7 dB under). The first play after power-on differs from a program-load render by about −24 dB (not isolated). About 2027 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.

CHAPTER III — MOONSHINE

Dark fantasy & atmosphere. On screen: the Moonshine scene, accent Foam White; hold a note and the dog howls. Drones and slow pads — these want long amp releases to survive the house hard-chop. (Live, a held-open gate helps: REC is HOLD since v0.2, so press it with the notes down and they keep sounding until you press REC again or STOP.)

  • 17 Titanic — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved as is; variant B of Batch 2A). The chapter anchor.
  • What it sounds like: Cold, heavy and hollow: two saws a fifth apart, steady rather than seasick, with a deep sub-heavy floor. Low notes open up and ring out big; high notes close down and go dull, so the weight lives at the bottom of the keyboard. Dry, desolate, and it hangs on after you let go.
  • Sound design notes: Low — roots and fifths around A1 to A2, where it opens up; played high it is dark and dull, by design. Every note is two voices, so POLY 6 plays a three-note chord in full and a fourth note steals. It is a held-note patch: the release is long (about 1.3 s to silence), so quick chopped notes overlap (not auditioned on a fast riff by ear). It ships dry; the spring is clearly audible on it (about 5 dB under the dry sound at DRAIN 60, mostly harmonics above 150 Hz — frozen or muddy is a matter of taste, untested by ear). Tape (CHEW) is an optional garnish for a dying-tape feel, at noticeably more CPU. Tricks untested on this patch.
  • 18 Roto-scopo — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved; variant D of Batch 5A). A moaning dungeon drone.
  • What it sounds like: A low, dark drone: a square tone with a second square an octave below it, played by three slightly out-of-tune voices. A resonant low-pass filter opens and closes slowly and unpredictably by itself, so the tone moans and drifts without a knob being touched. Dry: no echo, no spring. It lasts only while a key is held.
  • Sound design notes: Hold a key, the sustain pedal or REC (HOLD); the release is about 2.7 s nominal. One note at a time: a chord plays only its last key, and legato does not restart the envelopes. Best in the low register (judged on A1 and A2 holds of 15 s). A short tap is much quieter than the held note because the attack is slow. The wander is one shared random LFO on the cutoff; the engine has no Poly-Mod, so the movement cannot follow OSC 2 (measured on A1: the centroid ranges 316–708 Hz, a 14-semitone range). Slop is at the knob's top (VINTAGE 127). About 1897 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.
  • 19 Micro-mist — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved; variant D of Batch 5A round 2). Replaced "Blackwater", a sub-bass patch dropped on 6 Nov. Neon pixels floating in the ether.
  • What it sounds like: A soft-attack chord in the mid-to-upper register: a saw with a slightly sharp square an octave above it, through a band-pass filter. It hovers on its own echo and a large spring, and keeps hanging in the air for several seconds after you let go. Bright rather than low, and it does not flicker or scatter: a held pad dissolving into its effects, not a granular texture.
  • Sound design notes: Chords work (POLY 6). The mist after key-up is the effect tail, not a latch: a held chord needs the key, a sustain pedal or REC (HOLD). After a 10 s chord the tail is 20 / 40 / 60 dB down at 1.6 / 4.1 / 5.8 s. The spring leads the echo (first repeat 3.9 dB under the spring). Short notes are faint (a 150 ms chord tap is 8.7 dB under the held chord). Nothing sits under 150 Hz, so it is not for low notes. Not a real granular engine: no freeze, reverse or pitch-shifted repeats. The LFO is set but inert at these values. About 2000 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.
  • 20 Fire & Ice — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved; variant D of Batch 5B). A soaring fantasy solo.
  • What it sounds like: A single-voice lead that tears into every detached note with a bright hard-sync sweep, which then settles into a rounder line. It is pushed into overdrive and thrown into a long, ping-ponging echo that sits on top of a short spring. Notes slide into each other a little.
  • Sound design notes: MONO, one note at a time. The sweep fires on detached notes; played legato the sweep is not re-fired (centroid over the first 100 ms of a riff: 3610 Hz detached against 1573 Hz legato). The sweep survives the filter (CUTOFF 84). Glide takes 94 ms for an octave step. The echo is a free 374 ms (FEEDBK 92; the first repeat is 10 dB under the note) and does not follow the tempo. Drive is GROWL 48. About 1967 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.
  • 21 Cowl Shadow — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved as is; variant C of Batch 2A). A brass wall that blooms.
  • What it sounds like: A brass wall that starts dark and soft and swells open while you hold the note: a quiet murky hum that, in a few seconds, blooms into a wide, full, glowing brass, with a slow drift inside the stack. Dry. When you let go it fades out slowly and darkens as it goes.
  • Sound design notes: Hold the note. The bloom takes about five seconds (a tenth open at under a second, nine-tenths at about four, measured on A2). A sustain pedal or REC (HOLD) should hold it open the same way (not tried on this patch). Release early and it never opens — let go at 2.4 s and it is still dark and just fades in about two seconds; after a long hold the release takes about a second to drop 20 dB and about four to vanish. Legato doesn't restart the bloom; release and play a new note. It sounds quiet if you tap a note: short stabs read about 13 dB under the bloomed level. One note at a time (five-voice unison). Measured only on A2. Tricks untested; a little DRAIN would add depth (untested).
  • 22 Melting Orb — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved; variant D of Batch 5A). A dignified collapse.
  • What it sounds like: A thick stack of detuned saw tones that opens bright when the key goes down and then slowly sinks: the filter closes and the pitch falls together over a few seconds until the sound settles low and dark. A held collapse, not a zap. Takes chords (three keys gate six voices). Dry.
  • Sound design notes: Hold the key; the melt happens while it is down (the pitch ends about 6.8 semitones lower, 90% of the fall at 4.0 s on A2). A short tap hears only the bright opening. On key-up the melt partly runs backwards: pitch and brightness climb back through the fade (not tested whether it is audible). OSC 1 is off, because ENV>O2 bends OSC 2 only. A three-key chord peaks at −4.1 dBFS. About 2489 host instr/sample worst case, the highest of any voiced patch on the host yardstick. Tricks untested.
  • 23 Crypt Dust — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved; variant D3 of Batch 5B round 2). Frail, crumbling atmosphere. (Brief changed after listening; it was: noise + thin pulse, heavy tape wow, no drive. The final patch has no tape and only a trace of noise.)
  • What it sounds like: A thin, narrow pulse run through a band-pass into a pale, dusty tone, with only a trace of noise under it. The level flutters slowly and irregularly, in steps. A short echo and a large spring blur it. It rises slowly when you press a chord and hangs on after you let go.
  • Sound design notes: A held-chord pad (POLY 4: all three keys of a triad sound); short notes are faint (a 150 ms chord tap is 13.7 dB under the held chord). The noise sits 24.4 dB under the pulse. The chord peaks at −4.0 dBFS, which limits VOLUME. About 2065 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.
  • 24 Fugue State — VOICED (Nov 2026, approved; variant C of Batch 5B). A dizzying pad.
  • What it sounds like: A soft, dark, triangle-like pad whose pitch trembles quickly, wide in the stereo field. Each chord runs into a short echo that feeds back on itself while the pitch is still moving, so the repeats sit at slightly different pitches from the notes being played and the chord smears. A spring adds a further tail. No filter movement, only the pitch and the echo.
  • Sound design notes: A held-chord pad (POLY 5). A triangle LFO at 4.9 Hz moves the pitch by ±178 cents; the echo is 144 ms at FEEDBK 95 (10 repeats above −40 dB). The tail is 20 / 40 / 60 dB down at 1.6 / 3.5 / 4.6 s. Runaway tests show no clipping. One shared LFO, so no true rotary. The kill switch clears the echo buffers (not tested here). About 2038 host instr/sample worst case. Tricks untested.

CHAPTER IV — ACID CAN

Prophet-5 survivors, rebuilt by ear — never ripped from factory data. On screen: the Acid Can scene (a tipped-over can oozing acid in an alley), accent Acid Chartreuse. All eight patches (25–32) are voiced.

  • 25 SAWTOOTH — VOICED (4–5 Nov 2026, approved as is). The iconic poly-brass, a Prophet-5 survivor rebuilt by ear.
  • What it sounds like: Two saws a few cents apart, stable and warm, with the filter swelling open on each note and settling into a solid, brassy body. It holds still: no wobble, no chop, only a gentle vibrato that fades in if you hold a note.
  • Sound design notes: Low-mid to mid register; chords and fifth-and-octave voicings are home ground (each note is one voice; three- and four-note chords should play in full — not yet chord-tested). Medium to long notes show the swell best: it peaks about 84 ms in, so a very short stab catches only the start. It is the stable counterpart to 03 Half-Life. The vibrato arrives after about 1.1 s on held notes; LFO PITCH to 0 removes it. Ride the ALGORITHM for a tired-string-brass wobble; Tape Stop as a swell-out ending (both untested on this patch). All effects are at 0 on purpose: a dry brass, with a spring or echo yours to add.
  • 26 BSyncA — VOICED (11 Nov 2026, approved after listening; variant D of Batch 6A). A ripping sync solo.
  • What it sounds like: A hard-sync lead built from three slightly detuned voices that beat slowly against each other, with a master oscillator you can hear underneath the synced one. Every detached note starts with a bright sweep that tears down into a duller body; it is pushed into drive and left dry, with a short glide between notes. Played legato, the sweep does not come back.
  • Sound design notes: UNISON, one note at a time: three voices all play the key you press and a chord plays the last key only. The sweep fires on detached notes: on notes 2–8 of the riff, the centroid over the first 100 ms is 2935 Hz detached against 1742 Hz legato. The sweep was measured on A3; the riff runs A3 to C6 and nothing else was measured. The drive darkens the strike: GROWL 44 lowers the crest factor from 11.7 to 6.0 dB, and the centroid over the first 50 ms is 2662 Hz against 4165 Hz with no drive, so the brightness of the rip trades against the drive. GLIDE 50 takes 64 ms to come within 50 cents of a legato octave step. Dry: no echo, no spring, no tape. VOLUME 90, −18.05 dBFS RMS on the lead phrase, peak −11.0 dBFS. About 2326 host instr/sample worst case (GROWL about +595 of it). Tricks untested. The original brief had a silent master oscillator, one MONO voice, no drive and an echo with a spring; the brief is kept in the presets doc.
  • 27 R3V3RT — VOICED (11 Nov 2026, approved after listening; variant G, a calibration render of C with a longer filter decay, chosen by ear). Tight, immediate analog bass.
  • What it sounds like: A single-voice bass from one pulse wave. Each note opens with a bright filter snap that falls into a lower body; the body holds at a steady level for as long as the key is down, and when the key goes up the note stops almost at once. Played legato, the snap is not re-fired and the notes after the first have no front edge. Dry.
  • Sound design notes: MONO, one note at a time. The snap fires on detached notes: on notes 2–8 of the eight-note line the first 20 ms centroid is 2200 Hz detached against 154 Hz legato. On A2 held 1 s the level is 2.0 dB under the peak at 100 ms and 3.4 dB under at 300 ms; after key-up it is down 20 / 40 / 60 dB in 11 / 15 / 19 ms. Low register: A1's fundamental is 55 Hz, and only 17% of A1's body energy is above 60 Hz (99% on A2), so a low A1 is mostly inaudible on a small speaker. VOLUME 98, −18.00 dBFS RMS on the low riff, peak −13.8 dBFS. About 1379 host instr/sample worst case, not lighter than the original (1377). Tricks untested. The original had a saw plus a sub-octave pulse; the sustained single-pulse body is what Vincent asked for.
  • 28 Arr 2 Dee 2 — VOICED (11–12 Nov 2026, approved after listening; variant D2 of Batch 6B round 2). Renamed from "Bell Tolls" at Vincent's request; he asked for "Arr Two Dee Two", which is 15 characters against the 14-character name field, so the on-screen name is "Arr 2 Dee 2". The brief changed after listening: the original was an inharmonic FM chime set against the hard-chop gate; Vincent asked for a bell ring with body, healthy decay and sustain, a clean base to shape live, and no top grit.
  • What it sounds like: A sustained, struck bell tone built from two saw waves with a mid-frequency sideband character. It rings for several seconds, a slow shimmer moves its pitch and level, and a small echo and a spring sit behind it. It is dry of drive and tape.
  • Sound design notes: The key you press is the bell's hum, the strongest partial; the prime is an octave above it, so the strike may feel an octave above the key (not measured as perceived pitch). The five classical bell partials (hum 0.5, prime 1, tierce 1.2, quint 1.5, nominal 2) are all present; at A4 in the first 300 ms they read 0 / −7.7 / −11.1 / −10.5 / −13.6 dB. It rings on after key-up: a note released at 400 ms falls 20 dB in 3012 ms and 40 dB in 5610 ms. The ring of a held note to −40 dB is about 5.8–6.0 s across A2–A6, and the level is within 1.2 dB across the keybed; A6 is bright (21.3% of its first-20 ms energy above 4 kHz). POLY 5; a three-note chord reads −21.0 dBFS RMS, peak −6.0. A fast eight-note run peaks at −4.03 dBFS and sets the level limit. Live shaping (it sits mid-range on CUTOFF 88, X-MOD 32, ENV>O2 64, OSC 2 FINE 64, echo MIX 45, DRAIN 35, CHEW 0): CUTOFF and X-MOD change the brightness without moving the partials; echo MIX, DRAIN and FINE barely move the ring; ENV>O2 ±10 breaks the bell, because the tierce falls from −10 dB to about −47 dB at either side. The top grit of the first version was the FM, not CHEW or GROWL (neither is in the patch). Not carried: a crystalline tail (the engine has no per-partial envelope). About 2118 host instr/sample worst case; riding CHEW 45 or GROWL 44 on top reads 2901 or 2713, and both 3496, on the host yardstick. On the FM-1 (12 Nov), with all four Psych Chain effects pushed hard, four notes held read about 4500 µs against the 5800 µs budget in the source (Vincent's reading, ±100). Tricks untested.
  • 29 i scream — VOICED (11 Nov 2026, approved: variant D with CHEW 0). Built by ear from Vincent's field recordings of a real South African ice-cream van; nothing is sampled. The exact version was not heard before approval (Vincent heard D with tape and approved it without).
  • What it sounds like: A bright, struck chime built from a square wave with a second oscillator that zings down in pitch at the strike. The ring decays slowly, over a couple of seconds, and a gentle slow shimmer in pitch and level fades in after the strike and sways the ring. A small slap echo and a touch of spring sit behind it, and everything passes through a narrow, honky mid-band like a small horn speaker. There is no tape in it. Vincent hears it as closer to an arcade or vintage video-game chime than to finger cymbals (his ear, not measured); the bank had nothing in that register before.
  • Sound design notes: Voiced for A4 to A6; nothing outside was measured. The ring of a C#6 falls 6 / 12 / 20 / 40 dB in 252 / 550 / 1030 / 1896 ms, so with notes 580 ms apart several rings overlap (POLY 5). A three-note chord (A#5 C#6 F6) plays whole and is the loudest phrase (−21.3 dB RMS, peak −4.06 dBFS): use it as a wind-chime. The shimmer is a TRI LFO at 0.8 Hz (the engine has no sine). The filter is a band-pass peaking at 1099 Hz. No tape: CHEW is 0, so no wow, flutter, hiss or dropout. VOLUME 113, −17.9 dBFS RMS on the chime melody. About 1863 host instr/sample worst case. On the FM-1 (12 Nov), with all four Psych Chain effects pushed hard, four notes held read about 4500 µs against the 5800 µs budget (Vincent's reading, ±100). Tricks untested.
  • 30 THE DØG — VOICED (4–5 Nov 2026, approved; variant H of round 2). The signature patch, and the flagship.
